utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Registrar, could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. I see that all the accused are here. Defence teams have been informed that Mr. Ostojic can't be with us the rest of the week, that he will join again next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The same for Mr. Krgovic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And I see that you are alone, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Sarapa will be here on Monday as well. Or Tuesday, rather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. The rest of the teams seem to be okay. Prosecution, Mr. McCloskey on his own, together with his case assistant. Are there any preliminaries on your part? None. Okay. I'll pass on some information. For those of you and also for the record, for public consumption, less than an hour ago we handed down a decision on the Prosecution's third motion for leave to amend Rule 65 ter Exhibit list. Are you all aware of this? You are. So I don't need to state anything else on that. Now, you will recall that there is pending confidential Prosecution submission to the Trial Chamber's 12 September 2006 decision on Prosecution confidential motion for admission of written evidence in lieu of viva voce testimony pursuant to Rule 92 bis. This was filed on the 9th of January. The submission of the Prosecution identifies the specific written evidence of Witness number -- Witnesses number 77 and 81, which the Prosecution proposes for admission pursuant to Rule 92 ter. Prosecution also proposes that Witness -- Witness 81's statement be admitted in unredacted form. There is also a purported explanation that intercept one in Annex A of its November 21 motion had not been included in the Rule 65 ter exhibit list because the focus of the Prosecution had been on a different time period. The current submission also gives some indications as to the relevance of this purported intercept. Now, I'm raising all this because Witness number 77 will testify soon after the one who is starting pretty soon, and Witness 81 even before him. So what we have decided to do is because of the urgency of the matter, we are turning on to you to see whether you would like to make any comments on the Prosecution submission of the 9th January. Actually, reminding you at the same time that none of the Defence teams had actually objected to the conversion of the status of Witnesses 77 and 81 from 92 bis status to 92 ter. So basically the only issue remaining is essentially whether good cause has been shown for the addition of the intercepts you are all aware of to the Rule 65 ter exhibit list. So I hope I've made myself clear. If there are any questions, please do address them now. Do you wish to comment on the inclusion or insertion of the purported intercept in the 65 ter exhibit list even though or notwithstanding that it had not been therein included earlier? Are you satisfied with the good cause which the Prosecution believes it has shown? Yes, Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I would just like regarding the 9th of January motion by the Prosecution, we would like to be given some time in order to present our answer either by the end of the working day this evening, today, or tomorrow in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll take it up again tomorrow, but please do put us in the position when we can decide the issue before Witness 71 -- Witness -- not 71, Witness 81 starts giving evidence. You will be using this intercept with Witness 81 or with both?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, just with that witness, but I don't know if the witness will need to discuss the intercept. He doesn't, of course, I don't think, remember it, but it was one of that witness's intercepts, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. I thank you both. So we'll visit that again tomorrow. Now, we have been working and basically concluded our in-camera discussions on another motion, and the decision is more or less orally prepared, but we need to give it a final visit tomorrow or later on today. This is decision on motion for Prosecution witnesses one of whom is due to start very shortly and that is Witness number 69. We can here now inform you that although Witness 69 was included in the latest Prosecution motion for protective measures, his fate as regards protective measures had already been decided by us way back in November. So there is no change to that. We can safely proceed with admitting Witness number 69, and he will start giving evidence very shortly, enjoying the same protective measures he had earlier on pursuant to a previous order from a different Chamber, and that is voice distortion, facial distortion, and pseudonym. All right? The others will be dealt with in a written decision that we hope to be able to hand down tomorrow sometime in the morning or later on today if we have -- find time to go through it. I think I have covered -- yes. I've covered everything that I needed to tell you for the time being. Sometime in the course of next week, this is very possible that we will convene a 65 ter meeting in camera, not here, to discuss the future planning of the case. We've had time over the recess to examine thoroughly what has been happening over the past months, and I think it will be useful for everyone to meet and exchange a few views on the matter. Last point I wanted to raise is the following: One of the things we touched upon before we broke for the recess was the question of the satellite images or whatever they are, and, I have enjoined particularly the Defence teams to try and respond to Mr. McCloskey, to the Prosecution, or give a feedback to the invitation that he had extended to you with a view to passing on your specific requests to the US Embassy for further action. Has there been a development in this regard? We just want to know, that's all. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic approached me briefly and we had a nice chat about the possibility of him perhaps not having to talk to Mr. Butler, but everyone -- that was as everyone was leaving. So I'm hopeful, but we'll have to continue whatever discussion he may have. No one has asked me to help them with the United States Embassy. They are, I believe, still open for requests, if there are any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So I take it when Mr. Ostojic returns next week you will take the matter up with him again with the understanding that he will be speaking forth rest of the Defence teams and not just for the Beara Defence. We need to registered some progress in that area, because time is flying and the sooner it's resolved the better it is. Okay. Can we bring in the witness, please? I think you need to bring down the curtains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir. Welcome to this Tribunal. You are about to start giving evidence. Our Rules require -- you have given evidence before. Anyway, so you know what the procedure is. Madam Usher is going to give the text of a solemn declaration which you are required to enter before you can start giving evidence. Please read it allowed and that will be your undertaking with this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I thank you. Please take a seat. Make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm going to explain to you very briefly what's going to happen. The Prosecution has asked on your behalf that you be granted some protective measures. We have granted you the same protective measures that you enjoyed in the previous trial, namely the use of a pseudonym, voice distortion and facial distortion. I suppose these have been explained to you and you are satisfied with this arrangement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey will go first, and then you will be cross-examined by the various Defence teams. Mr. McCloskey, please, since this witness will be testifying with voice distortion, it's important that before and while he is speaking all other microphones are switched off. All right? Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And like we have done in the past, can I seek leave to sit down during the questioning and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problem, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Ms. Stewart will be behind me with a sharp pen if I don't hit the mike. But could we start off first with -- if the witness could take a look at the pseudonym, which is P02338 and tell us if that's him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Only the first letter of my name is different on the paper, but other than that my name is on the paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. Can I have a look at it please. All right. Sir, I'm going to give it back to you, and you will be given a coloured pen. Could you please make the necessary correction and give it back to the usher. So thank you. That will go under seal, and we'll give it a number later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you recall providing information to the Office of the Prosecutor on May 5th, 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes. I gave a statement on May 5, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have you had a chance to read that statement in the last day or so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is the information on that statement true and correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if you were to be asked in -- similar questions or the same questions would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I will stand and read a short summary of that statement. The witness is a Bosnian Muslim and was born in Zenica in 1955. In 1979 and 1980, he performed his mandatory military service with the JNA. Prior to the war, the witness lived in Bosnia and worked as a mining engineer. In 1992, he joined the BiH army and served as a regular soldier in the area of Mount Majevica until August 1994 when he was then selected for a position with the Electronic Warfare Unit of the 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, just a moment. May we go into private session for a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption. Yes. We are in open session again. I apologise to you again for the interruption, Mr. McCloskey, but it was necessary. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. He was then selected for a position with the Electronic Warfare Unit of the 2nd Corps and was based in the northern site of operations, as it's been referred to in this Tribunal and as he has referred to more specifically in other statements. On joining the unit, he received a one-month course with about 30 other individuals on the basics of radio technology, the use of various radio equipment, and how to tape record radio communications. After this course, he was stationed in the northern site along with about 15 other soldiers. He began his work at the northern site as a regular soldier. He worked on a 7- to 10-day shift with a maximum of 10 other people at any one time. Some people would monitor conversations while others were resting. Due to the shortage of quality equipment, it was it only possible for two to five people to listen to radio traffic at any one time. While on duty, the witness would listen to radio conversations, tape the important ones, and then transcribe the conversations from the tape into books. These conversations were transcribed into the books by listening to them multiple times. After taping a conversation, he would normally write it into a notebook as soon as practicable. It was normal to listen to conversations for two hours and rest for four. He would normally finalise his work after the two-hour period. After writing the conversation in the notebook, he would hand it over to someone for typing. He had nothing further to do with the conversation or proofreading the typed version. In early January, 1995, he was appointed shift manager. In this role, he continued his same work with the additional responsibilities of organising logistics, discipline and other matters. He recalls working during the fall of Srebrenica in July 1995, and recalls that there was not much radio traffic at that time and his main concern was the route of the refugees who were leaving the enclave. The witness recalled some conversations from the Srebrenica time period including a conversation where a BiH commander named Semso Muminovic was requesting to meet with Vinko Pandurevic and a conversation where someone from Konjevic Polje was asking for an excavator from Zvornik. The witness stated he was able to recognise several voices of people he heard over the radio, including General Simic, General Tolimir, and General Zivanovic. The witness was asked what the term "Zlatar" meant and he stated it was the name of the Drina Corps headquarters in Vlasenica. He also recalled that the code name for the Zvornik Brigade was Palma. The witness recognised the code name Panorama, but at the time he was questioned by the OTP he could not recall what it stood for. The witness was aware that the state security was using the same location and doing similar work in 1995. Okay. That -- that ends the summary. I have a few additional questions and a few specific intercepts I would like to ask the witness about, and -- but for the record, his 92 ter statement is P02337. And if I could sit down, it will help me turn this machine off when I need to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, Witness. Can you briefly give an outline of your educational background for us, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go into private session for this, Your Honour. This section may -- may be helpful to be in private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sure. Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you explain to us why you feel the handwritten version is the more accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: The version that I wrote is more accurate. As for what happened to the typed or printed versions, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall working with a typist in getting a time version done or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: It was very rare. It didn't happen, practically, very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. But can you -- you cannot discount that it may have happened at times, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Very rarely. It happened very rarely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we have a small problem here with the translation. The witness said "skoro nikad," "almost never," but the way it was interpreted was, "No, not very often," but the witness said, "almost never."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you referring to page 14, line 1? Because what I have there is it was very rare. 14, 1, no?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot hear the attorney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It didn't happen practically very often. And according to you it should be? "Almost never"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said that this did not happen, that this hardly ever happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness, you've followed what Mr. Zivanovic has pointed out. Do you agree with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It means that this cooperation is not ruled out but it very seldom happened. The degree of that cooperation and the way it can be expressed as hardly ever or not often or almost never, it's just a degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the sense of my remark was that the witness said "almost never." I mean, we can interpret that in different ways, but this is what the witness said, "almost never."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can close the matter there. That's clear enough to me. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to try if we could to go over some of the -- the intercepts and ask you a couple of questions about them. If we could start with 65 ter 1198, and if we could have the printout version in B/C/S. I don't think we -- people could refer to their -- their packet. That's 1198C for translation. The translation is not the main point here on this particular question, but it might help. And if we can blow that up so that it can be seen. Let's keep going down slowly a bit so we can -- we're looking for a word, "Kovacevici," or something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, is this being broadcast? No? All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I may have given the wrong number. No, it's 1198. Excuse me. Okay. Could we keep going. Sorry, I'm not mixed up. We need to go to the next page. Keep going down, please. Okay. You can stop right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The conversation I'm directing your attention to is this one that says "kanal" or "channel" 5, and we see the word down at the bottom, "Kovacevicima." And this has been translated to: "At 2006 hours Blagojevic reports that 50 men left and he has 60 more down in Kovacevici." Now, could we go to the same conversation in the handwritten format. And that is 1198A. Okay. And we -- if you could take a look at that, I think it's clear to everyone that we don't see anywhere in this intercept any reference to Kovacevici, and I can read the latest intercepted -- or the translation that we've provided everyone. "At 2006 hours Blagojevic reports that five minutes or half an hour ago 50 men left and that he has 60 more down there in reserve." That's 1198 D. That's a revised translation. Now, I know it was a long time ago, Witness, but do you know -- do you know how "Kovacevici" got put in the printout version as opposed to "in reserve" in the handwritten version that you wrote?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to another one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, do we have those documents in our binder or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, you should, and we -- we've got the -- the translations are -- are pretty new, and they just -- they just came in. We worked those out with the witness in the last day or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Actually, I couldn't find the B/C/S version in tab 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: I had the same problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we might have -- we might have missed it. Yes. It's not tab 11, it's tab 13 in your version. You have a more updated version than I do. So you'll find it in 13. There was a few additions, and it -- it changed our numbering system. The original ones we gave the Defence should be tab 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My index says that tab 13 is 65 ter 1201. There should be some mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. You're correct. I am the one that's not updated, and -- but hopefully we'll be able to sort that out, and I'll try to make that clear as we go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In e-court system your number was right, 1198.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Janet's right, you're right. I've got my old notes, so that's the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to -- it's a conversation dated 16 July at 1529 hours, and it's 11 -- 1192 should be the 65 ter number. In your packet it should be 7 -- Defence, it should be 5, if you've got an old one. Six. And if we could put on the version, the handwritten version which is 1192B. Sorry, 1192A. And if we could go down to the very end of this -- this -- keep going to the very end, the next page. All right. Now, in you could follow it in B/C/S. I will read an English translation to part of this, which I hope will get to the issue I'm trying to get out, and that is starting with the line: "Well, the line is down. I can't hear you at all. Hello. Wait a minute. Wait a minute. Have Vinko, that. Since we heard that 01 had said it." Now, if you could find the B/C/S version of that. The problem here is that the letters 01 can be view two ways. They can be viewed as 01 or O-N by the way it's been written. And the word "on" means "he" in B/C/S. Can you tell us by looking at your handwritten version whether it's an O-N or a 01?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I can't be sure. That was a long time ago. I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, there's a -- let's go to other intercept of 15 July, 0828 hours, which will be 65 ter 1170, and we might as well go to the printout version of this, which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It should be tab 3, Your Honours. It's 1170C. If we could blow that up just so we have the beginning of this conversation. Scroll down a bit. Okay. Down more. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, in looking at this conversation in the top we see Jocic, question mark in parentheses, X, Y, Pero. Then if we look at the conversation, can you tell us looking at that conversation how many people are talking to each other based on this transcript?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: The way it is put here would make me conclude that there were four participants, but, but I don't think this has been transferred to the computer in a proper way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, up at the top it says Jocic. Do you know -- can you relate Jocic to any other -- any of these either X, Y, or Pero? This Jocic, should he be viewed on his own?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: As a rule, if something is in the brackets and if there is a question mark, then the person transcribing is having doubts as to the identity of that person and ascribes another sign to that person, namely the X.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So who then is Jocic ascribed to based on your knowledge of this intercept and experience?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I don't have my original text here. Therefore, I can only assume based on this that Jocic is the X.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's to the -- go then to the original. If we could go -- that will be the same number, but it will be the letter B. Sorry, letter A. Okay. Now we have the hand-written version up there. Does that help you determine if this name Jocic can be ascribed to any of the participants, X, Y, or Pero?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Jocic should be the X.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Let's go to 15 July intercept dated -- well, time of 0834 hours. It should be 65 ter 11 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before you proceed. Perhaps you can have him clear this up. Looking at the same document, handwritten document, and following up on what he's just stated, that Jocic is the X. Now, the first line after that is crossed. Then there is X saying , "Alo." Then Y, who says either -- "Alo." Then X says something, and Y says, "Dobro." And then it's X and P and X and P and X and P, et cetera. But how can he explain or stand by his explanation that X and Jocic -- all right. I think there might be an explanation. No. Let's me take that back. I think it is understandable as it is. Okay. It is understandable as it is. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And again, if we could go to what is 1171. Let's go to the handwritten version. It's tab 4, and the handwritten version is B. It's at the bottom, and it's very short. It should be under that time I gave. Yes. And just to try to be helpful, this says X and Jevdevic, and then it says X: "Semso Muminovic is asking for V. Pandurevic to call him on 14985."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, this doesn't appear to be a question and answer that we see most of the time in these notebooks. Is this summary as I would call it, is that what it is, a summary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: That is correct. It is just a very brief summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you explain why you would have summarised a conversation as opposed to writing out the -- what was said as we've seen in other notebooks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Seldom did it happen that one needed to extract an important piece of information out of a seemingly unimportant conversation. Should an information crop up during a conversation and the conversation is unimportant as a whole, whereas that one piece of information is, then we would just make a very brief summary as a rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to one last area, and I think this will be easiest to go on the ELMO. I want to show you an original notebook, and we'll get some help with the -- the ELMO. And the original notebook is P02343, and it has various ERN pages on it. And if we could go to ERN page at first 0781721. And I've actually marked it with a little -- it should be the first little blue sticky there. And if -- we'll put this on the ELMO and you can take it look at it, but basically it's a simple question. As we were going through some of these notebooks, I noticed that there was a name, Fuad, written over some of the handwritten entries and usually in a different coloured ink. And this, we now have that in front of us. Can you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we better -- I think we -- we better go into private session on this Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was thinking about that, Mr. McCloskey. Let's just do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we are in open session now. Mr. McCloskey has finished his examination-in-chief. Mr. Zivanovic is about to start his cross-examination. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you kindly advise the witness to allow a short interval between question and answer, and could I also invite you to do the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask you to pause after my question for a few section before you provide your answers so to enable the interpreters to interpret accurately and timely. Could you tell me which type of devices you had at the facility where you were one of the shift leaders or squad commanders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I cannot recall all types of devices, but we had tapping devices which used tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me how many workstations were there in the facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Between two and five workstations in the room we worked in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever compile any reports about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: About the number of workstations, no. No reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show Exhibit 1D128 to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't have it in the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please zoom in a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I don't know which document it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see that it's a document with the radio relay listening station and its name in the heading of the document, and then there's the date, the 18th of February, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also written: "Subject: Review of workstations with the accompanying equipment"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see that there are three workstations there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see that each of those workstations has the appropriate equipment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can I just ask for the next page to be shown, please. Do you see the remark? It was all right just a little bit before. A remark where it says: "All equipment are serviced by one operator." And also the range of the equipment is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me. If I could just make sure we're not transmitting this. I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just made sure that we are not, in fact. Thank you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's how I understood it as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I see the remark that all equipment is serviced by one operator.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we look at the next page, please, of this document. Could you please zoom in at the end of the page. Can you see it's a document you drafted? It says: "Section commander."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes. My name is signed here in this version, but I do not recall drafting this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me something about the antennas that were used at this facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I can tell you very little. It was a long time ago. I've forgotten 90 per cent of all those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you -- are you knowledgeable about antennas in general?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: We did have some hours on antennas in our course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question referred to you personally. I'm not talking about the whole group now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I have basic knowledge about antennas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please now look at Defence Exhibit 1D127? Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No? Can you please tell me -- well, you see that four antennas are listed here. They're described as operational, and then your name is signed at the bottom. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now show the witness Defence Exhibit 1D149.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before I forget, Madam Registrar, please do remember me and you, of course, that these two documents that have been referred to need to be put under seal. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see this document now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you also see that it also refers to antennas, their outside circumference and depth? And I can see that this report was again submitted by you. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, do you remember at all if you had any problems with antennas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I don't recall any particular problems with the antennas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how the antennas were placed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I cannot remember it in detail, but I know that these were just regular antennas placed in the direction of the devices that we were listening to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall having problems with antennas because of the wind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at Exhibit 1D140? It's a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As you can see, this is a report on radio reconnaissance or surveillance. Can we now look at the bottom of this page? Can you please look at the remark. It states: "During measurements outside it was very windy so that the antennas were moving a lot." And then there is a comparison of what the deviation is and so on, and then the signature is of the commander of the section.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I cannot recall the particulars in these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the beginning of this document, please? Do you see that this is September 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I haven't said anything, but I'm finding it hard the relevance that the wind is blowing antennas a bit in September 1995. I understand these are documents, but I just ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you wish to remark on that, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I would like to remind Mr. McCloskey that he presented evidence about the antennas being placed on pillars or pylons, and I will get to that, but the question really should indicate the time period when these posts or pillars were being used. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I stand to be corrected by my colleagues obviously but the relevance is that there may be the possibility of point proving because of these problems proper monitoring of conversations was not possible. Is this what you -- what you're trying to -- okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Do proceed, but go straight to the point, please, Mr. Zivanovic. If you have a particular period in mind in particular, go straight there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honours. Could the witness be shown Defence Exhibit 1D131.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And any time it is convenient to you, we should have a break in about four minutes', three minutes' time. Any time you choose, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please scroll the page down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see that under paragraph 1 in this dispatch it says: "To install the pillars as soon as possible and set up the antennas"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please scroll this document to the beginning. Does it say the 20th of November, 1995, in the heading of this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the heading of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we can go on the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into open session, please. I think we were in -- okay. Let's go into break for 20 minutes, please. Try to be as punctual. We need to recover as much time as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We don't have any estimates that I'm aware of -- of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I do have estimates. The Popovic and Miletic teams, 45 minutes each; Beara, 25 minutes; Borovcanin, 20 minutes, Gvero, 15 minutes -- sorry, yeah, and 15 minutes it's Nikolic and Pandurevic. This is what I have. I mean, with some sense of practicality, we should finish with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We don't have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. I'm hopeful, optimistic we should finish with this witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we ask those to be sent to us, and we also have not received any indication of what you might be using for cross-examination. This can be troublesome and there is no translations for some of them. I think we're okay, but just a reminder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have make allowances. I think most of the components -- members of the Defence teams have just arrived like we have, so these are minor leniences that can be forgiven on this occasion at least. So we'll have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Monsieur Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me if your unit had prepared plans for anti-electronic warfare prepared in advance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I was not informed about any plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me which zones or areas were monitored by your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: The zones changed. We surveyed the area of the Drina Corps, the Bijeljina Corps. These were the two main areas. Sometimes the focus would shift to areas where there was combat, and that's where we would be monitoring the traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me if you remember when you received the order to direct your systems to the Drina Corps area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I cannot recall that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you to look at Defence Exhibit 1D154, please. Can you see this document? And can you see that in paragraph 1 it says: "All antenna systems or equipment to be redirected to the monitoring of the Drina Corps and the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps areas of responsibility." Do you agree that's what is written here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: There is the possibility that that order existed, but I do not recall receiving it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And that it had the instruction to operate on the Zvornik-Vlasenica-Han Pijesak and Srebrenica-Bratunac-Vlasenica frequencies.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes. This did take place, but I really don't recall the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we scroll the page up so that we see the top of the page, please. Can you see the date 8th of August, 1995, here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me whether your unit sent reports on radio reconnaissance for specific months?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I don't recall such reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement that you gave before you came to testify as a witness, I saw, and you repeated in subsequent statements, things about notebooks. You said that notebooks were received from the command and that they were filled when they were full. Then you would receive new notebooks. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes. That's how it was for a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that new notebooks would not be opened for as long as the current notebook had space to write in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I also saw in your statement that the notebooks were used from February 1995. Until then the notes were made on pieces of paper. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now clarify one thing, please? There are certain numbers on all of the notebooks. Can you tell us who assigned those numbers? Perhaps I can remind you. There was a notebook that was shown to you that bore the number 92. Another one had the number 29. Do you know who assigned those numbers? Was that something that was done in your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I really don't remember exactly how that worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you do it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like us to look at two intercepts that you transcribed that are in the notebook. This is exhibit of the Prosecution from the 65 ter list with the number 1001.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 1201, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in the tab system it bears the number 8. No, actually not number 8. It's tab number 13.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could the counsel specify A, B, or C, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Judges' tab 15, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thirteen we already came across before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In the Serbian it is 00800633. I believe this is the letter B, the document marked with B.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You've recognised this previously as being your handwriting. I wanted to know this: Can you recall whether you heard this conversation clearly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I cannot remember whether I was able to hear it clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will not press this any further then. Could you please look at another intercept. It is number 1224. In our folder it is tab 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Judges' tab 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is B. Could you please scroll down the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is this particular intercept. You've also recognised this as being your handwriting. Could you please look at page number 2. Could you clarify the remark for us, the underlined item. It says: "In the background one can hear French."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay. Go ahead, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you recall and explain to us what this was about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: In this particular conversation one could overhear the French language. There was the original language of the participants, and in the background one could hear a male voice speaking French. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at the previous text with the conversation itself, you will see that we have only one participant. As far as I understood, you were unable to hear the other participant. If you wish, you could -- you could look at the documents so as to be able to remind yourself of the entire contents.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I -- I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, when you say that in the background you can hear French, does it mean that it was the other collocutor or was it at the place where the person whom you could understand was? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: If you cannot hear a certain participant, then you cannot hear his background noise. Therefore, the French must have occurred at the place where the first person was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, it was at the place where you could hear that -- where the person whom you could hear was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Have you agreed amongst yourself who is going next? Mr. Meek. Mr. McCloskey, if we could -- you know, because the days and the weeks and the months will pass, and we'll need to return to these documents, obviously, and also the index that accompanies them. Could you instruct someone from your team to provide us with an updated, correct index; in other words, reflecting the documents as they appear behind the respective tabs?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Ms. Stewart has got that. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. How are you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I'm fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you. I would like to ask -- or confirm with you that your educational background which you previously talked about had nothing whatsoever with the electronic warfare that you found yourself involved in, in 1994 and 1995 in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: You are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Further, I want to make sure I'm correct in -- on this position, that since you had been a common soldier in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina up to the time in August of 1994 when you were shifted over to the electronic warfare division, your duties as a common soldier prior to that time also had nothing whatsoever to do with the electronic warfare in which you found yourself in August of 1994; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Could you please tell me and tell the Court where it was that you obtained the 30-day training of which you've testified?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I attended the training in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us, please, approximately how many trainees were with you during that one-month period in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: There may have been around 30 or slightly more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And with 30 or slightly more trainees, how many individuals did you have training yourself and the other 29 or 30 trainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Well, we had the practical and the theoretical part, and the practical part was attended by everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And the theoretical part was not attended by everyone, then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I said that during the theoretical part we were all present at the same time, and when we had practical exercises we were then split into groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: How large would those groups be, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly. Between 5 and 10. There were three centres, so each group would comprise some 5 to 10 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness, when you say 5 to 10 men comprising a group, that would be a group of trainees such as you being one of those men. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: You are. Our group would then attend some practical exercises.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you're in the -- we're speaking of the theoretical groups; correct? Pardon me. The practical part of it, you had 9 to 10 students or trainees. How many individuals would you have training this group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: The practical part of the training was conducted in the centres which trained other people besides ourselves. Therefore, we used their instructors. I don't know how many they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, I'm just trying to ask. I'm trying to clarify that if you were in a group of 9, 10 or 11 trainees, you have no independent recollection today if you had one instructors or two instructors?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: We attended the training at the surveillance centre. There were several people there. I don't know how many exactly, though. And we worked with those men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall during the practical aspect of the training at the centre, was it such that each trainee had an instructor such as one-on-one, or would five, for example, trainees have one instructor, or would all 10 of you maybe in a group have one instructor? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I understand your question. Sometimes there was one instructor per three men. It was never on one-to-one basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It was also at times 1 on 10, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I don't think we ever had such a situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Perhaps you can't do this, but can you give me an average of the trainees in regards to how many people were training them on the average during this 30-day period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I'm afraid we are talking at cross-purposes. We are talking about the theoretical part where the whole group was present, and then there have the practical part when we were split into groups. That's how we attended the practical part of the training.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I apologise. Perhaps the question was -- is worded improperly, because we were talking about the practical training and I was still on that issue. So in the practical aspect of your training, what was the average trainee -- number of trainees per person training, or persons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: It was two to three men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, since you had the -- both types of training, can you tell me, did the practical aspect of this 30-day training encompass what percentage of that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Not much, I think. Perhaps some 20 per cent, not more, although I cannot tell you anything more precise than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So would it be a fair statement, then, theoretically -- the theoretic training took up 80 per cent of that month as opposed to approximately 20 per cent of practical training; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: The theoretical part comprised most of the training, much more than the practical aspect. Therefore, such a ratio could have been in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And if I understand the statement which you gave the OTP in 1999 well, the folks that were training you were not experts, were they? They were just merely civilians with some knowledge in this field and other colleagues with some knowledge of the field. Isn't that a fact, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: The composition was mixed. There was civilians and some people who worked at various places. But in any case, there were some civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you will agree with me -- [French on English channel].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm receiving French. That possibly can be corrected now. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: But you will agree with me, Witness that during this 30-day or one-month course which you went to with 30 other individuals, you were not trained by any experts in this area but only by civilians and colleagues who had some knowledge about this type of interception activity. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I beg to disagree with your assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And tell me how you disagree with that, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: All the people who came were knowledgeable about the things they taught us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, I'm not going to disagree with you that in your statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 5th of May of 1999 that you stated in regards the 30-day training, the one-month training period, and correct me if I am wrong, that this -- you were taught the basics of radio technology; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: We were trained in basics of radio technology and other areas important for the duties we were to perform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, when you gave this statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 5th of May of 1999, weren't you endeavouring, Witness, to tell them in the greatest detail possible what that one-month training had been comprised of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I don't have my statement before me, but I believe I said it covered several areas. I may have omitted some, but I did make an effort in specifying that there were some -- several areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness, I'm just going to read this to see if I can refresh your recollection and move on. You told the Office of the Prosecutor on 5 May 1999 when you were interviewed, quote -- and this would be the third paragraph down in your statement, quote: "On joining the unit, I was given a one-month course where I learnt the basics of radio technology. This involved using the equipment and how to tape material. The training was run along the lines of a school with colleagues and civilians who had knowledge of these topics training us. While I was training there, there were about 30 other students." Does at that refresh your recollection, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And everything that I just read out, were all of -- of what you just mentioned, the several areas covered during this training. Put it all in there, and I just read it all to you out of your statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: The notion of radio technology is a very comprehensive area which could be broken into several parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would you agree would me that the -- that the notion of radio technology is very comprehensive area and it can be broken into a lot more than several parts? It can be broken into many parts. Wouldn't you agree, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And when you went to this 30-day course and it was run like a school, did you go to classes Monday through Friday, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly the way the curriculum was organised in terms of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you recall, Witness, whether you had days off, or were you in class every day for 30 straight days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I think we were off for one day a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And on the days you weren't off, can you just generally, to the best of your recollection, tell the Court, please, approximately what time you'd start in the morning and what time you would break for lunch, what time you would then reconvene in the afternoon, and what time you would finish that day?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, I can assure you we're being very, very, very patient allowing you to proceed with this line of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And I'm about done, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But there is a limit, and I think you've just exceeded it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yeah, and I understand Your Honour's position. I just would like the one question - I'm done with this - how many hours a day did he spend in the training. If he can tell me. If he can't, fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Come on. Let's round it up as soon as possible, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Can you estimate how many hours in a day you were training? How many hours a day would you train when you were training?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: It could have been between six and eight hours a day. Not more than that, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, just one series of questions or one issue here. Before -- either during the training or before going to the location where you were intercepting these communications in July of 1995, were you ever briefed on how you should determine whether a conversation was one of interest that you should tape as opposed to one that you shouldn't tape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: There were remarks made on how to decide or how to pinpoint an important conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Can you tell me where the remarks were made and give me an idea of one such remark?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: During the classes there was a topic which had to do with the analysis of data reaching the operational centres. The operational centres sought a certain level of quality of information, and we were asked to provide that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You've answered me about how you were supposed to ascertain quality or give quality level of information, but you haven't answered my question that I put to you, and that is: Were you ever briefed or told or taught how you should determine if a conversation would be relevant and worth taping? How was that done?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: It was precisely the goal of the theoretical lecture to try and explain to us what was important for us to decide on, whether to tape a conversation or not. A large part of our training was dedicated to that specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You'll be glad to hear I'm about done, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, were you ever briefed on any individuals in your area of coverage where you were located before you went, the name of any individual you should be on the lookout for, for example? Key players from the army of the Republika Srpska or your enemy at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: The focus was not on individuals. The focus was on the approach to the professional tasks at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Could you explain that answer a little bit for me? You say you didn't want to focus on individuals, but the focus was on the approach professional tasks at hand. Could you explain that a little more for me? I don't understand it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Well, if we hear there is a General participating in a conversation, then must be important because otherwise he wouldn't bother to call. On the other hand, if we have a simple citizen calling, of course we were probably not going to get as good information as we would from a conversation, including a General.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. And during your training you were not given any instructions, or you weren't taught or shown or -- any tapes to listen to of known voices of certain generals from the Republika Srpska army, were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Precisely. It was a collective training for the army of B and H, not for a specific corps or area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Then how much -- if you can remember, how many of the 30 soldiers who trained with you ended up in the same location as you in 1994 and into 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: There were several courses, and out of the group that I was a part of, I was the only person who was at that particular location.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: In your statement of 5 May 1999 to the Office of the Prosecutor, you told the Prosecutor's office that you were able to recognise several voices during the conversation -- conversations during that period. Do you recall telling them that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And did you list each one of the individuals whose voice you believe you could recognise or did you leave any out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I didn't list all of the people. I just mentioned some characteristic ones. I couldn't recall all of the persons or the voices of all the persons. At some point I could recognise the persons, but not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Back in 1999 with the OTP, you told them that, for example, you could recognise General Simic, General Tolimir, and General Zivanovic, those three only. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, are there any more as you sit here today, understanding that everything was fresher on your mind in 1999 than it is here in 2007? Are there any other individuals who you would recognise their -- them by their voice when you were in the field?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: There were some individuals, but it's an operations part of the job. These are people who are always doing that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, is it a fair statement that you were never -- during any of this training, you never had any specific training on how to recognise voices of the enemy that you might capture on tape. True?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: There was just a little bit on the techniques of listening to voices, of how you could recognise a voice because of the connection, but nothing on individual voices. Our training had nothing to do with individual voices but only the techniques on how to approach that job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And, sir, today, as you sit here today under oath, could you agree with me that this 30 days of training that we've just discussed is wholly insufficient and at yet for the job they sent you to do and that would, if you had to do it all over now you would run a much more thorough and longer course?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I would not agree with you, with your conclusion. For each job that you do in your life, nothing is ever long enough or sufficient, in principle. For the job is that we were doing we received certain knowledge that we used and that we applied in order to do the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Meek. Who is next? Mr. Bourgon, who is appearing for Mr. Nikolic, will be cross-examining you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Some of the questions I wanted to ask were already covered, so I will try to keep it as short as possible, and my first question deals with the -- the notebooks. And with respect to the notebooks, I would like you to confirm that regarding the numbers that were assigned to these notebooks, and regarding the dates that were assigned to the notebooks what they would arrive to you and the date that was put at the end when a book was completed, that you did not keep any written record of this exchange of notebooks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: It's correct that I didn't keep any record of it. The command would take the notebooks, and that was the job of the command. It wasn't my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, when you testified in the Krstic case, you were asked some questions regarding these notebooks. And just to summarise what you said then, I'm referring to page 4335, and that was at line 37 exactly, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Meek, you left your microphone on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry I had to interrupt you, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No problem, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll take this again, Witness. When you testified in the Krstic case, that was from your testimony at page 4335 to page 4337, at that time the Prosecution requested from you a confirmation that there was a date on every book that you received; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I cannot recall such a request.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Then without referring to the request itself, Witness, I would just like to know, can you confirm today that when you received a book from headquarters it should have had a date to begin this book. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: That's how it should have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you can agree with me today that it wasn't always the case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I agree with you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when the book was completed, that is when the final conversation went to the end of the last page of the book, then there should have been a date at the end to say that this book was completed, but also this did not always take place; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if somebody wants to find out the exact date of a particular intercept, this can only be done by using the first date and the last date of one of those notebooks. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you explain why this is not correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: All the conversations or the intercepts were transferred to the computer and sent to the command with the Paket radio connection, and all the information was also contained in the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe, Witness, my question was not clear enough. If I look at the notebook only and I want to identify the date of a particular intercept, it is necessary for me to look at the first date and the last date in order to be able to do that. That's the only way it can be done, using the notebook; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes. There is a problem if just the notebook is used.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I'll move on to another topic. It was -- reference was made earlier to your statement given to the Office of the Prosecution on the 5th of May, 1999. I would just like you to refer to part of this statement where you said, and I quote: "All conversations that were written down in the books were previously taped," and then you say, "and written down in the books from listening to those tapes multiple times." I would simply like to obtain a confirmation from you that it was always necessary to listen to a conversation many times before you could get a proper written version in your notebook.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: If there was a problem generally with an intercept or a conversation, then we would listen to it over and over. If there was no problem with the intercept, then it would be very quickly noted down in the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But what I get from your statement is that every time you had an intercept, it was necessary to listen many times to the tape because it's a difficult exercise. I'm simply asking whether you agree with me that it is indeed a difficult exercise in order to transcribe a conversation on one of those tapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you limit yourself to this new, different question, yes. Otherwise, he's already answered you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I keep this exact question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, repeat it, please, but stick to it, because the other question, the previous question, which -- with which you introduced your second question had already been answered by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Will do, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Witness, I'll say the question over again so that it's very clear. I'm simply asking, and I will read the exact question so that there is no mistake, and the question was whether you agree with me that it is indeed a difficult exercise in order to transcribe a conversation on one of those tapes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Sometimes it was easier. Sometimes it was the most -- more difficult part of the work. It's a very serious kind of work. It's not easy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will just refer you to an answer that you gave to Defence counsel, and that was during your testimony in the Blagojevic case, and I will quote here from the transcript at page 4078. That was in the Blagojevic case. The question was: "Would you hear a conversation more than one time if necessary before writing it down?" Your answer then was the following: "We faced a number of different situations depending on the quality of reception, depending on the pronunciation of the participants involved. Sometimes it was possible to transcribe a conversation after listening to it once or twice, but sometimes this took hours, and we needed help from our colleagues in order to be able to understand clearly what the participants were saying." Would you still agree with this answer that you gave then? Do you agree with this answer today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you -- in response to a question by my colleague from the Prosecution, I believe you said that once a conversation was noted down in a notebook and given to a typist, you had no involvement whatsoever with that conversation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: That was generally that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, moving on from the fact that this was generally the way, I would like you to confirm that even though you were the shift supervisors -- supervisor, sorry, you did not supervise nor review the conversations that were transcribed by the other people in your section?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there anything wrong? I heard -- okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the most part I didn't do that part of the work.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, again you say "for the most part," which appears to be different from what I read from your previous testimony. So did you sometimes do it, or did you never do it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I say "for the most part" because sometimes in certain circumstances I did encounter some documents. There was probably some reason for that. But in principle it was not something that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you recall any of these documents that you did have to supervision or had the opportunity to supervise, and why this took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I cannot recall the kind of documents that I was going to supervise, but we generally helped each other in situations where a conversation couldn't be heard very well. We would be helping each other in order to transcribe it. That was the point of doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I take it from your last answer, Witness, that you say that you would obtain the help of others in order to clarify a particular conversation, and that's exactly the point I'm trying to get at. When you did this kind of exercise seeking the help of your -- the help of people working in your section, would I be right in saying that the end result is you finally agreed on what is the content of the conversation by discussing with the others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: We're not going about it in the proper way. We were helping each other regarding understanding the pronunciation of certain sections of the conversation, not the content of the conversation itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I have to go back on this, Witness, because I'm not sure this is very clear, because this would agree us to understand that the person could understand the conversation but needed help with the pronunciation. Now, my understanding is that he could not understand what was being said, and he sought the help of other colleagues around him to try and find out what the conversation said. Is that the real version?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes, I can agree with you there. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if I look at a notebook, there's no way for me to tell whether a conversation falls in of category of I needed to listen only once or twice, or I needed to listen to the conversation for hours. I cannot tell by looking at the notebook, can I?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, one last question on the difficulties that were encountered, and again I will quote from your testimony in the -- this time in the Krstic case, and that is on page 4328, and that is from lines 10 to 16. The question was the following: "If you were unable to properly hear a conversation, what would you do?" This time your answer was the following: "There were many difficult situations. That is to say where we could hear the conversation but that there was a lot of interference and it was partly audible. But where the conversation was clear, the request was that anything we take down in written form should comply with the original. So if everything was clear, we would write it down. If it was inaudible or not clear, we would put three dots, and we did not write anything because we were not able to understand it sufficiently." My question to you in respect of this paragraph is that the methodology used about the three dots, what does that represent as far as you are concerned, those three dots, in the notebooks and the conversations that you took down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I cannot remember precisely how it went, but I assume -- I can just assume that there were pauses in the conversation. Maybe there were some things missing. But that's all. I really cannot remember more. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I appreciate your answer, because I remember that of course this is a long time ago. But can you just clarify whether three dots could in certain circumstances mean three worth, in other circumstances a pause, in other circumstances a longer blank in the conversation that you could not hear? Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: It could have different meaning, that there was a pause or that there was a word missing. I really couldn't say definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
