utterances.text: And would you agree with me, sir, that there was no real set standard as to what those three dots meant from one operator to the next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I cannot agree with you that there was no standard. "Standard" is a broad term, but in this case there were rules which we were all acquainted with when we came to the listening station.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me then make my question a bit more clear to help you out simply by saying that three dots for you in a certain intercept might not mean the same thing as three dots for another interceptor for another intercept. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Sincerely speaking I cannot remember what that exactly signified. We were all informed about the rules, but at the moment I cannot really remember what the significance of the three dots was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I appreciate your answer, and I appreciate the effort to go back all these years. I have one last question for you and that reference to something -- one of your answers when you testified in the Blagojevic case, and that was at page 4121, at lines 18 to 25. And the question this time came from a Defence counsel, and in your answer concerning one of your own intercepts, your answer was: "If this was faithfully transcribed, it means that that person was mixing two different kinds of dialect." But the part I want to quote from your answer is the following; the Defence counsel went on to say: "If I understand you properly, you say if this has been faithfully transcribed, if that is so, can I conclude that perhaps you did not," because this was your handwriting, "did not faithfully transcribe what you heard?" Now, your answer to this was the following: "There is always the possibility that a man makes various mistakes. Even if the same conversation is transcribed twice, these mistakes can be made. People are not robots. We only have identical copies made by computers. A person, a human being, can make a mistake." Would you still agree with this kind of answer today, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: That's how it is. That's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And one last question, Witness. All the time you spent doing those intercepts in that section, being the shift supervisor you probably were in a better position than the others even to see that, but my question is very simple. Were those stressful times, to do this job in a wartime scenario?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean when you say "better position." As the shift supervisor, I just actually had more to do than just the regular soldiers, and I also was required to take care of the soldiers a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe I will make my question more clear. For you personally, the job, the position that you held doing those intercepts, was that a stressful job in stressful conditions because it was the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: It was an exceptionally difficult job, and if you wish, it was stressful. It was a burden, a lot of work. All of these things were mixed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Allow a pause between question and answer so that the interpreters can catch up with you, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to put just some questions to you. I know we're tired and this has been going on for a while now. Your statement to the Tribunal investigators was given on the 5th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us other than the Tribunal representatives who was present when you were providing your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly all of the persons but I was summoned by (redacted) and he was there for a while or the entire time. I cannot recall, but he was present in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, can we move into private session for a moment because of the question that I'm about to put?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will are in open session, Mr. Stojanovic and Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When providing this interview, you were no longer a member of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the role or the task of the person whose name we heard a moment ago at the time you provided your interview, your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: In all honesty, I don't know what his role was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you recall whether during you are giving of the statement he made certain suggestions or had interventions or additions to some of your answers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I cannot recall a single such situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you were giving this statement, was he still an active member of the army and a member of the 2nd Corps of the army of B and H?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I think so. I know he was still in active service, but I don't know which unit he belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does the name Stefanie Frease mean anything to you? She was a representative of the Tribunal at the time you provided the statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I recall that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was she present when you gave the statement, when you were interviewed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I think so. I don't know whether she was there throughout, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your today's testimony during the examination-in-chief, you mentioned a person who belonged to your unit, and you said this person was a radio man. Without mentioning his name, can you tell me whether you provided any such answers to the Prosecutor's questions when you were asked what that particular person's role or task was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: When we are talking about radio men, their job was to transfer the intercepts into the computer and to use the so-called packet communication links to send them off to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave may we move into private session for a moment since we need to mention another person's name, and this person may appear as a protected Witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Stojanovic, let's move to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is this: This member of your unit, was he in the position to listen in to conversations, to note them down into the notebook, or was his job to transfer the transcribed conversations via Paket communication via the superior command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Perhaps on occasion he would listen in, but the gist of his role was to use the Paket communication to type everything into the computer and then transfer the data.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to ask you something which is unclear to me. There is a difference between the text sent to the command, the typed-out version, as we refer to it, and the handwritten version noted into the notebook by yourself. You said today that you believe the more authentic one is the notebook version; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You concluded that based on the fact that what was introduced into the notebook was what a given person heard when listening to a specific tape. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In your view, which would be the official version sent to your unit's superior command, the typed one or the handwritten one in the notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: The official version for the command was probably the one which arrived via the computer. They probably never saw my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me therefore that there was a possibility of an example used today by the Prosecutor, that the official version be less reliable than the version contained in your notebook; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes, there is such a possibility. We cannot exclude that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did -- at a certain point your superior command in those few days, not a year later but in those days, did the superior command have the opportunity to see the notes from the notebooks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I cannot tell you what the command did, but as for the notebooks, once completed and handed over to the next shift would go to the captain and taken to the command. As for who may have later referred to them, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And to conclude, I wanted to ask you this: At the location we termed the northern location so as not to mention the name, in addition to your unit there was some state security units as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes. There was a small crew.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The antenna systems at the location where you were, were they the same? Were they used for the surveillance of conversations by your unit as well as by the State Security Service? And I mean only the antenna systems.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I don't know. We did our job pursuant to our orders. The State Security Service pursued their own procedures, and I have no information as to what conversations they surveilled or intercepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I was unclear. I wanted to know this: Did both the army and the police use the same antenna system? As for who listened to what and which devices were used, I want to exclude that from my question. I'm only interested in the antennae. Did you use the same antenna systems?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I know that the service brought their own pillar and antenna, and we had nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that there were problems between your unit and the State Security Service? There was an investigation against your platoon commander specifically regarding these problems in the second half of 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I don't recall any investigation details, but at first the service began working with us, and then later on they separated and set up their own system.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the issue of using the antenna system and the investigation conducted against your platoon commander? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I don't recall that particular detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On two occasions today you said you could by that point recognise certain features of people's voices and recognise the given individuals. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you given any instruction as to how to keep register on the characteristics, on the features of voices of individuals? Did you keep any personal files, any date on the specific nature of how they speak, the words they use when conversing with people? Did you have any such files there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: As far as I know, no one told us to do any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You specifically as a section or squad leader, you were never given such an instruction in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And you did not keep any sort of files about those sort of people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: We kept no files. Data and analysis was not one of our tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will conclude with this question, and I will try to be as graphic as possible, because we've been in the situation to hear a number of people of your profile. You hear a conversation and the participants introduce themselves and someone at the switchboard says "Dragan is on the line," and then you would have the conversation. "Ljubo, how are you doing." "I'm fine." "How's your wife?" "She's okay." "How are you?" "I'm fine." And then they go on. Will you tell me something about the use of units, for example? In such a situation, were you instructed to write down only what you deemed important and specific for that conversation, or were you requested to note down the entire conversation including the greetings and formalities, introductions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: As a rule, the whole conversation should be contained. However, you offered a simplified version. If there is an interesting conversation, we turn on the tape recorder and it records everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Once that is taped and noted down into the notebook, do you make notes of the whole conversation or do you screen it and select the parts to be noted down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: As a rule, one should write down everything that was said. That's the rule. And if you have sufficient time on your hands, that is the best way to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you stand by that rule?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: For the most cases I stuck to it, although there were certain deviations, so to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your assistance. I have no more questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Madam Fauveau will be cross-examining you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Fauveau, go ahead, and we'll take a break towards quarter to 6.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, today you mentioned that it was absolutely necessary to get training for your type of work. I would like to remind you what you said in the Blagojevic case on the 7th of November, 2003 on page 4115. In that case you said for that type of job people got their training for 15 to 20 years in order to become specialists. Are you -- today would you say the same thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. That's a pretty rough paraphrase, to ask him that question, and it's difficult to even figure out what she's asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In order to answer you that we need to go to chapter and verse. Blagojevic, what -- which page, Madam Fauveau, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 4115. 7th of November, 2003, lines 19 through 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I suggest that someone reads it out. You can read it out yourself, Madam Fauveau, to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, at the time you've said, and I quote: "[In English] During the month of training my knowledge of equipment was very basic. Usually people are trained for 15 or 20 years to specialise in operating this equipment. We didn't have the time, and we did the best we could."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And reading -- and finish that answer in its entirety, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: "We made the best of it, whatever we could learn during the course, and we tried to apply the knowledge acquired during our training. Now how qualified or professional our work was, I think we need more time to tell. "I would" -- [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't have the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have it. "I would have been very happy if I had had 20 years of military education behind me when I started performing these tasks. That's all I can tell you."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, today would you confirm this statement? Would you say the same thing today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I think for any job and any person one needs the maximum of information and education, and the era that is before us requires permanent education of anyone. It means that one needs a lot of time for any type of work, although I cannot say that the job we did was not done well. It was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it exact to say that the unit in which you were in 1995 did not have enough quality equipment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And can we say, therefore, that the equipment was often broken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I don't think we understand each other. If we are talking about the functioning of equipment, I claim that our radio devices were on all the time and that there were no interruptions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit 5D122. And I would like to mention that it's a confidential exhibit which contains the signature of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That will not be broadcast. And in any case, please, Madam Registrar, remind us all to make sure it's under seal, put under seal later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just -- just to comment. Perhaps it's a translation issue, but I don't think it has the signature of the witness. It has the name. It may have just been a translation issue, but it can be an important issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for pointing that out. It is evident from the document that we are seeing in any case. So let's go to the question, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I made a mistake, and in fact I wanted to say that this it exhibit contains the name of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that clarification, and let's proceed with the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, this is a report that you apparently have written because your name is stated on this report. Could you please look at page 5 of this document. We see very clearly that on this -- page 5, we see the following: "[In English] Discussing in our work the following was said: The equipment we're using is old making for frequent breakdowns, and it is difficult to get spare parts for some equipment under repair." [Interpretation] To refresh your memory, it would be good if the witness could be shown page 1.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No microphone, Mr. President. Could Ms. Fauveau repeat her question in the microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your microphone is switched off apparently, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: At the very beginning of this document, you can see that this is a document dated the 21st of February, and that in fact it is a document which talks about a certain person that came to visit belonging to the 2nd Corps, and he was in the zone in which your unit was deployed. Now, I would like to ask you, firstly, do you recall that this particular person whose name appears on this document, do you recall if he came to visit your unit in fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I recognise the situation you're referring to, and I remember the gentleman. I don't remember all the details, though, but I remember him being there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you recall drafting this report yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I cannot recall that. I know there were some questions that I needed to respond to concerning his visit, Mr. Tasic's visit.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What I just read to you under 5 -- under number 5 on the second page, is this an answer that you gave following a question that the gentleman whose name you mentioned asked you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I think our superior requested that we inform him about the situation. I don't remember any details, but requests were made constantly, particularly at the time when he took over the unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whenever it's convenient for you, Madam Fauveau, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have maybe one or two questions on this topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, can we therefore say that you would not have lied to your superior commander and that what is described in this report reflects the truth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: In principle I never lied to my superior. I'm not a person who would lie, but I cannot recall any details pertaining to this situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, maybe this is the right time for the break then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Because we had a redaction we need 30 minutes. How much more time do you require, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About 30 minutes, Mr. President, maximum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Haynes, where do we stand with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Touch and go, but should just finish this evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, allow me now to ask you a few questions on the tapes that you were using to tape the conversations. Is it exact to say that you were using those tapes over again once you finished a conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: There were different periods, different situations, but generally we did use the same tapes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it exact to say that you were not sending the tapes systematically to your superior?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I said that there were different periods. In one period we were sending them there, but then in another we were not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it exact to say that in July of 1995 you did not send tapes to you superior command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes, I think that that was the period when we were not sending them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you were using the tapes, would you first erase the conversations that were taped or would you tape a new conversation on top of the conversation that was already taped on that tape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly which technique was applied. I really cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it exact to say that your unit had to listen to conversations but also to scrabble them, that they had those two duties?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Our job was to listen to the conversations, but this term, "decoding," I don't know what it means.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Allow me to read to you exactly what you said in Blagojevic case on page 4074 on the 6th of November between lines 9 through to 14. In that case you state and I quote: "[In English] Basically the unit had two objectives. The only objective of the unit was to protect it the population and the military. This was done by electronic surveillance which in this case came down to listening in on conversation being transmitted to enemy frequencies, and interfering with the enemy's communication which was less often the case." [Interpretation] Is it exact to say that you were interfering in the conversations, that you were perturbing or disturbing the conversations of the enemy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I have to say that there were two sections. I was in the listening sections, and I had my colleagues who were -- whose task it was to interfere during certain conversations.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit 2D48, please. This should be a confidential exhibit because it contains the name of the witness. Could the witness be shown page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Under number 5 you can see how many people worked for your unit, and 5.02 you can see the name of one person that was described as Ometaci, which means the scrambler or the jammer. Did your section dispose of such a person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: My section did not, but the command sometimes assigned different people to our facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And for the person under number 5.03, was that the person that was in charge of sending reports to your command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes. The communications person under 5.03 was the person who did that work, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, that person that was in charge of communications, was that person a member of your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes. That was our radio man.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And that person, was he subordinated to the same commander as yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes. I think that he was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know the person under number 5.02, the scrambler, do you know who -- under whom he was, or he was subordinated to whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I can assume that he was in the same command, but -- I think that he was in the same command, but I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, do you know if your command insisted mainly on the content of the conversations or was the number [as interpreted] of participants as important, equally important?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, there's a mistake in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: It's name, the name of the participants, and not the number of participants.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Everything is important in a conversation. Information is important as well as the participants. Again, I'm saying something that may not be my job, but let me say this: Everything is important.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many notes were used at the same time, those -- how many booklets were you using at one time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the correct or the exact number of notebooks, but the principle was to use one notebook per equipment, but sometimes it would happen that there were a few notebooks that were being circulated at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you wanted a conversation that you transcribed in the notebook be transcribed in the computer, would you bring that notebook to the person who was in charge of drafting it on a computer? Would you bring it to that person, in that person's room where the person was working?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: That's how it was for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And can you tell us where was that person physically? Was that person in another room, and where was that room with respect to the room where the people who were listening to conversations were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: We had several rooms. The communications person's room was next to the listening room.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Was there a door, a direct door between the room where you were for intercepting conversations and the room in which this person was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: All the rooms were entered from the corridor, so the entrance to the room where the communications person was from the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could any person enter the room where the person was in charge of communications?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: As a rule the communication person should have been alone, but sometimes colleagues would go in.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And in your team, the team of which you were the chief, how many persons were in charge of communications?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: It was always one person for our unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, if I understood the system, sometimes the conversations which were urgent should be immediately sent. If there was only one person, how could this person work 24 hours out of 24?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: One person worked. How they worked for 24 hours, well, they work that time. There weren't information -- there wasn't information constantly throughout the 24 hours. When they worked, they would sit at the computer and they would work.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What I'd like to know, was it possible for an interceptor exceptionally to enter information into the computer and send them? I would like to ask you whether exceptionally --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I didn't hear the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You need to repeat the question because there was a problem with the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to ask you whether exceptionally an interceptor could replace the person charge of communications and enter the data into the computer and send a report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I don't remember. There were situations when a communications person replaced an interceptor, but I don't remember anything the other way round.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like now to have 2D45 shown to the witness. Exhibit 2D45. Could you show the lower part of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, I understood you said that you rarely had had an opportunity to see the report before it was sent, but when a report had your name on it, did you have an opportunity to read it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I did not read that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Have you ever had the opportunity of seeing a report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I don't remember any occasion like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown the top of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity sometimes to see the seal, the rectangular seal which is in the angle of the document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: No, I didn't have the opportunity to see that stamp, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And do you know to whom the reports like this one were sent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I don't know what happened after the radio person. I would say that that would be the end of my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In the Blagojevic case, on the 6th November, page 4079, you said that you were not in charge of analysing the conversations, and other people were in charge of analysing the conversations or intercepts. Could you say who was in charge of analysing the intercepts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: What I know, what I heard, is that there was a centre at the corps command that used to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit 2D47.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, just after the goods which are in this room or the equipment which is in this room, there is a sentence which says that on the basis of data declared in the report it was possible to evaluate the size of a unit. Do you agree that this sentence is already a form of analysis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Move to the next question, Madam Fauveau, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, you said a while ago that you were not aware of the intercepts done by the state security. On this exhibit, you can see the words "CSB SDB Tuzla." Could you explain what these words mean in this report sent by your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: From what I know, these are abbreviations for the public security centre and the State Security Service, if what I know is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that this particular conversation was transcribed from the service of -- security of the state services?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I think that that is so. I assume that it's so, but I don't remember whether it was precisely that or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you spoke to the Prosecution office on the 19th of May, 1999, for the second time, you said that the 21st and 25th divisions were very active in monitoring conversations. Were the 25th and 21st units located in the same locality as your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were not at the same positions. The 25th Division listening unit was in a completely different location.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And the 21st?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: The same. But when the combat activity stopped, then those two listening units fused into a joint section, but that was towards the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I still have a last question to ask.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown again 2D48, Exhibit 2D48. Could the witness be shown the third page.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, under number 6 there are requests, requests for equipment which you had sent to your command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes, I see the requests.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And if you look at those requests, you will see at a given moment you ask "UNPROFOR tyres." Could you explain what that means?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: It says here, "raw rubber from UNPROFOR." There is a difference between tyres and raw rubber.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Does this rubber, raw rubber, you got it from UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I don't know if there was any cooperation with UNPROFOR in relation to any kind of equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember why you wrote "raw rubber of UNPROFOR," why you wrote that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I don't recall writing or drafting the report, and I certainly don't recall the particulars.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no other questions to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Madam Fauveau. Mr. Haynes for Pandurevic. I skipped you --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were right to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Your Honour, let's see if we can do this in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: As I understand the situation, whether any particular conversation was relevant was a matter which was left entirely up to the individual operator; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that each of you had two or three pieces of machinery to monitor, each of which monitored a number of different radio channels. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: We had different situations. The tendency was one piece of equipment per soldier, but if we didn't have enough people, then more people would -- one person would cover more workstations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So the first stage of the process was, the operator had to decide which piece of equipment to listen to if he had more than one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: If a person was monitoring several workstations, then they would be listening to all of the equipment there. There would be no difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And having decided what was relevant to listen to, he then had to decide what was relevant to record?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: What was recorded -- well, if a person could not monitor a conversation, it would be taped and then listened to later. If he decided that something was interesting or potentially interesting, he would turn on the tape recorder, which would then be listening instead of him, practically.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And whose decision was it to transcribe or, alternatively, summarise a conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: The person who listened to the conversation would decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And were you given any instruction on that as to whether a conversation should be fully transcribed or merely summarised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: There were some conversations or discussions on this topic, but generally speaking it was up to the person, the interceptor, to see which conversation would need to be transcribed and which would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you ever recall being discouraged from transcribing a conversation? In other words, be told not to do it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I think that we didn't have any influences. The decisions were ours. Individual decisions, or if we worked together in the shift then sometimes we would discuss it together, but there were no elements of influence in this at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on. Now, when particularly interesting or urgent information was received by you, what was the procedure for most quickly delivering it to your command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: In particularly urgent situations we would use a wire connector even an open telephone, but the best option would be to mark the conversation as urgent and send it off like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to ask you about Semso Muminovic. He was one of your commanders, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Do we redact this or --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm confident that's a name that's appeared openly several times already in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So let's proceed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you want me to repeat the question, Witness? Semso Muminovic was one of your commanders, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: For just safety's sake, I will go into private session for this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Would have you have been able to recognise his voice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't think so. We never intercepted his conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, that's what I was about to ask you. I was going to ask you whether you ever heard him or someone you believed to be him whilst you were monitoring radio traffic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't remember hearing his voice ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I can show you the document if you -- if you wish, but on the 15th of May of 1999 you spoke to a lady called Stefanie Frease, didn't you? I'm sorry, 16th of May.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I don't know on what date we spoke, but there was a conversation with her back in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: This was the occasion upon which she showed you some of the notebooks that you'd used in recording conversations. Do you recall that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes, it was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you were asked then whether you -- there were any particular conversations you remembered. And these are her notes. I'll make that clear. You she said you concerned a conversation about opening a corridor. "It was a call made one of our commanders, Semso Muminovic." Do you remember saying that to her?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I forwarded that information, and I discussed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, what I want to consider is in the light of that and remembering that conversation, do you think now you actually did hear Semso Muminovic when you were monitoring conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I don't think I heard the voice. I don't have the document before me, but that information came from the enemy. It didn't come from our side, from our devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, your particular responsibility during the period with which we were concerned was monitoring the movement of refugees who'd left Srebrenica, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Our surveillance area was Podrinje, but I always thought it important for all of us to follow the movement of those people and to see that they get out safely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And were you aware through any of your briefings or intelligence that you received while you were doing your job at that time whether Semso Muminovic had the same concerns as you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I forwarded the information I picked up on the enemy lines. As for what was happening objectively, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to move on to another topic. In monitoring the channels that you did, did you notice any particular patterns of usage by the enemy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How frequently did certain enemy units change channel, a lot or not very frequently?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I think it happened seldom. Some units stayed on their respective channels for quite a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I know it's going back a long time, but in particular do you remember the usage of channel 3? Was that something that was easy to monitor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I cannot recall that specifically, but I don't think that that particular channel presented much difficulty for tapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, going back to what you said to Stefanie Frease on the 16th of May of 1999, you remember conversations about the opening of a corridor, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: That is correct. I remember it nowadays as well. This conversation was on the enemy communication lines, and there was a mention of this information concerning a corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Are you talking now about a conversation or more than one conversation over a period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I apologise. Right here and now I can tell you that I can recall two such situations. The first one being that we picked it up from the enemy lines concerning Mr. Muminovic's request, and in another conversation Mr. Oric was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And are those both conversations that you recorded on tape and then transcribed or summarised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I don't have that material before me to view it, but as for the Muminovic conversation, this was a very brief piece of information. As for Oric, as far as I remember that conversation was noted down in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Again, I know it's very difficult to remember, but when in May of 1999 Ms. Stefanie Frease showed you some books containing those conversations, did you see one or both of those conversations in the books you were shown?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I think I saw those intercepts in the notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were they in one notebook or more than one notebook that Ms. Frease showed you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: You're going into great detail. I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's fair comment. I simply wondered whether you could help me. Now, I'm going to try very quickly in the time we have available to turn to some of the intercepts which you made notes of, and the first is our P1170, and can we start with A. That's the original book, please. This is at tab 3 in your packet. You've seen this before. This is the intercept -- it's in your handwriting, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes, this is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And it's the intercept you've been shown before in which it appears that there are at various stages four speakers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, that misstates the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'll just carry on. We've got a little amount of time and objections really don't help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When he testified, he made it clear that Jokic -- or Jocic equals X. Okay? Anyway, anyway, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The objection is perfectly valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What appears in the third line there is that the X or Jocic wants to speak to somebody called Travera Pera; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: That's what it says here, and I assume it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that's somebody who he believes can get in such with Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: You're going into analysis of the conversation. I can read out what I see here. That's all I can do. But, yes, it seems so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And then X says: "Hello again," and you start using the letter P then. Is that because you identified a different voice to the Y you were using him speaking to before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: That's what it was most likely. A third collocutor appeared, and I assigned the letter P to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for -- to clear something up that's in the English translation, the word "travar" means having to do with herbs in Serbian, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I don't know. I put down Traver. I don't know whether it's got anything to do with herbs or whether it's merely a nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's very helpful because on the English translation there is a little enigmatic section, but that's what it is. The word Traver means herbs or herbalist and the English translator has put in their own interpretation. Now, towards the bottom of that intercept, two lines up from the bottom of the page, so can we go down. Information is being given that Vinko is being sent over there to his men. Again, that's something you wrote down, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I wrote down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can you recall now whether this was information that you treated as particularly urgent and conveyed it to your command as quickly as you could?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129
utterances.text: I can't recall that particular detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not going to finish tonight. I'm very sorry. I've done my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problem --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problem. We'll continue tomorrow. How much more do you expect you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: About 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So you will have the next witness ready tomorrow, and we'll need to finish the cross-examination, see whether there is anything else, and then the documents or exhibits, and then we can start with a new witness. I thank everybody. We will reconvene tomorrow at 2.15 in the afternoon. Thank you. Have a nice evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 11th day of January, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.01 p.m.,
